title: In-situ Monitoring of Automated Defect Formation in STEM
content: One of the very base forms of dynamic behavioral studies is the in situ examination of defect structure formation within materials. In this effort, through utilizing unconventional beam control and automated data analysis, insights into the formation of unique defect structures as a function of electron (e-) beam irradiation are revealed and the fabrication of different types of defects can be achieved. To accomplish this, the sub-Å sized e- beam of a scanning transmission electron microscope (STEM), following unique beam pathways, is used as a manufacturing tool for atomic-scale defect formation. Previous works have demonstrated that it is possible to fabricate unique nanostructures within 2D materials using similar techniques by precisely placing the e- beam [1-4]. In this study the formation of different defect structures within the transition metal dichalcogenide, MoS2, are studied, with the Mo6S6 nanowire-type (MoS-NW) edge structures of particular interest [5-8]. These metallic defects have been shown to alter functional properties within the semiconducting monolayer and, while the formation of these structures can be achieved stochastically with simple heating, more localized control of the formation of these structures can is needed to reliably form functionalized structures within 2D materials.
